Nine titles, in the approximate order each entered data and AI hiring. The dates are background — this sample runs {{< var jobskills.months >}} and can say nothing about when a title appeared — but everything after them is measured from the ads.

Across the whole sample, **30%** of ads require building or training a model of some kind and **42%** require calling a model someone else trained. That split is the thread running through these sections, and it moves with the chronology: the older the title, the likelier it is to build.

### 1. Quantitative Researcher — finance, 1980s–1990s {#sec-title-quantitative-researcher}

*47 ads, 2% of the sample*

The oldest title here, and the one that got there first. Investment banks and hedge funds were hiring mathematicians and physicists to price derivatives and find trading signals two decades before anyone said “data scientist”. Everything the later titles claim as novel — statistics on large datasets, models in production, money riding on the output — was already the job.

![](images/title-quantitative-researcher.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of the skills Quantitative Researcher ads require most often and the skills most over-represented in them, each against the share across all ads"}

**Take-home.** 15% of these ads want both a model and its deployment and 13% a model without it; the most distinctive requirement is quantitative research, and the nearest title is Data Scientist.

**Nearest neighbour.** Data Scientist (1.41 apart on the skills map), then Research Scientist (1.51). Furthest: Analytics Engineer (2.41).

**Build or call.** 26% build or train a model, 9% call one over an API, and 2% want the API work with no model-building at all.

**In the ads' own words.** The phrases most over-represented in this title, read out of the ads by a second model that was never shown our skill list, with the share of the title's ads using each: “finance” (10%), “large dataset analysis” (10%), “applied mathematics” (8%), “market microstructure” (8%), “portfolio construction” (8%).

> 5+ years of experience with quantitative modeling and pricing
>
> <small>— one of **3** Quantitative Researcher ads (6% of the title) that ask for “quantitative modeling”</small>

> Strong understanding of market mechanics and microstructure invariants
>
> <small>— one of **4** Quantitative Researcher ads (8% of the title) that ask for “market microstructure”</small>

### 2. Data Analyst — business intelligence, 1990s–2000s {#sec-title-data-analyst}

*309 ads, 11% of the sample*

### 3. Research Scientist — industrial labs, long-standing; current AI form from ~2012 {#sec-title-research-scientist}

*160 ads, 6% of the sample*

The title is far older than data science — industrial research labs have used it for most of a century — but the version that shows up in this sample is the deep-learning lab role that followed the 2012 ImageNet result: publish, train large models, push the state of the art.

![](images/title-research-scientist.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of the skills Research Scientist ads require most often and the skills most over-represented in them, each against the share across all ads"}

### 4. Data Scientist — coined 2008, mainstream from ~2012 {#sec-title-data-scientist}

*518 ads, 18% of the sample*

Coined in 2008 by D.J. Patil and Jeff Hammerbacher, then leading data at LinkedIn and Facebook, and made famous by the 2012 *[Harvard Business Review](https://hbr.org/2012/10/data-scientist-the-sexiest-job-of-the-21st-century)* piece. The pitch was a hybrid: enough statistics to be rigorous, enough code to be self-sufficient, enough business sense to be listened to.

![](images/title-data-scientist.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of the skills Data Scientist ads require most often and the skills most over-represented in them, each against the share across all ads"}

![](images/model-and-ship.png){fig-alt="Stacked bars per job title showing the share of ads requiring both a model and its deployment, a model only, deployment only, or neither"}

**Take-home.** 49% of these ads want both a model and its deployment and 17% a model without it; the most distinctive requirement is classical ML, and the nearest title is ML Engineer.

**Nearest neighbour.** ML Engineer (1.10 apart on the skills map), then Research Scientist (1.19). Furthest: Analytics Engineer (1.81).

**Build or call.** 55% build or train a model, 35% call one over an API, and 12% want the API work with no model-building at all.

**In the ads' own words.** The phrases most over-represented in this title, read out of the ads by a second model that was never shown our skill list, with the share of the title's ads using each: “regression” (6%), “clustering” (7%), “statistical modeling” (10%), “data science” (31%), “causal inference” (15%).

> experimental design, causal inference and quasi-experimental methods
>
> <small>— one of **71** Data Scientist ads (15% of the title) that ask for “causal inference”</small>

> Expertise in machine learning and predictive modelling

> <small>— one of **35** Data Scientist ads (7% of the title) that ask for “predictive modeling”</small>

### 5. Data Engineer — ~2011–2014 {#sec-title-data-engineer}

*341 ads, 12% of the sample*

### 6. ML Engineer — ~2015–2016 {#sec-title-ml-engineer}

### 8. Forward Deployed — Palantir-era term, mainstream from ~2023 {#sec-title-forward-deployed}

*434 ads, 15% of the sample*

A solutions-engineering lineage with a newer name. The engineer is embedded with the customer, building and adapting the product in front of them. The term escaped Palantir and spread as AI vendors discovered their product needed fitting to each buyer.

### 9. AI Engineer — ~2023 {#sec-title-ai-engineer}
